reading.title: Ways People Hold On to the Past
reading.purpose: Learn the words for the objects, places, and feelings that connect us to earlier times.
paras: People have many ways of holding on to the past. Some are big and public, while others are small and private. Each one helps us remember who we were and where we came from.

A town may build a monument, a statue or structure that honors a person or event. Each year, people gather there to commemorate the day with songs, speeches, or a moment of silence. Scientists may also dig up a relic, an old object that survives from a much earlier time, such as a clay pot.

At home, memories are smaller. An heirloom is a valuable object passed down in a family for generations, like a grandmother's ring. An antique is an old object, often more than a hundred years old, that collectors may value. A keepsake can be much plainer, such as a ticket or a dried flower, as long as it helps you remember someone.

When you travel, you might buy a souvenir to remember the place you visited, like a postcard or a small magnet. Later, looking at it may bring on nostalgia, a warm and sometimes sad longing for a happy time that is over. Friends often reminisce together, talking happily about trips and holidays from long ago.

A person's legacy is larger than any object. It is what someone passes on to the future, such as kindness, a skill, or a garden that others will enjoy. Objects help us remember, but values and actions can last the longest.

choices: a statue that honors a person or an important event
a ceremony held once a year to remember a special day
a small object that someone buys on a trip to a new place
an old object that survives from a much earlier time
qs.why: The text explains it directly: a relic is "an old object that survives from a much earlier time."

qs.q: Which sentence tells what nostalgia is?
choices: When you travel, you might buy a souvenir to remember the place you visited, like a postcard or a small magnet.
Later, looking at it may bring on nostalgia, a warm and sometimes sad longing for a happy time that is over.
People have many ways of holding on to the past.
Friends often reminisce together, talking happily about trips and holidays from long ago.
qs.why: This sentence names the feeling: a warm, sometimes sad longing for a happy time that is over.

ev.text: Later, looking at it may bring on nostalgia, a warm and sometimes sad longing for a happy time that is over.

qs.q: How is a keepsake different from an heirloom?
choices: A keepsake must be more than a hundred years old.
A keepsake can be plain and does not need to be valuable.
A keepsake is always bought on a trip to a faraway place.
A keepsake has to be handed down for many generations.
qs.why: An heirloom is valuable and passed down, but a keepsake can be as plain as a ticket as long as it helps you remember someone.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Only very old and valuable objects can help a person remember.
Families should never throw away anything that belongs to the past.
Towns remember the past better than families or single people do.
People use many kinds of objects and customs to remember the past.
qs.why: The reading moves from monuments to family objects to travel souvenirs and ends with a person's legacy, all ways of remembering.
